resources.string: Completion records your choice. Your playing has not been assessed.

For intervals and scales, 1 is the selected reference note; for chords, it is that chord\'s root. Degrees follow the reference note\'s major scale. ♭ and ♯ lower or raise the same numbered note by a half step.
Standard tuning. String 1 is high E; string 6 is low E. Fret 0 is an open string.
Choose a major key on the outer ring. Its relative minor is on the inner ring. Explore the selected key\'s notes on the fretboard and play its example below.
Neighboring major keys share six sounding pitches. Compare them one step at a time.
Swipe sideways to reach every key.

TAB, or guitar tablature, tells you which string and fret to play. Read left to right; vertically aligned numbers are played together. e is string 1, B string 2, G string 3, D string 4, A string 5, and E string 6. 0 is an open string, played without pressing a fret. These examples use standard tuning; follow the practice instructions below for note lengths. In these exercises, 60 BPM means counting one beat each second.
Find C–D and C–E on the fretboard and compare their distances in frets.

Changing where you press a guitar string changes its pitch. Note names use A, B, C, D, E, F, G, then return to A. The same name occurs at different pitches. A note twelve half steps higher is one octave above.

On the same string, increasing the fret number by one raises the pitch a half step; two frets make a whole step. A sharp, ♯, raises a note a half step, and a flat, ♭, lowers it. Notes without sharps or flats are natural notes. Among adjacent natural notes, E–F and B–C are half steps; the others are whole steps.

An interval describes the distance between two notes. C to D counts two letter names, C and D, so it is a second. Its two-fret distance makes it a major second. C to E counts three names, C, D, E, and spans four frets, making it a major third. An interval name reflects both the letter order and the half-step distance.

Below, choose C as the root, the reference note for this comparison. Switch between major second and major third. On string 5, find C at fret 3, D at fret 5, and E at fret 7. Listen to each two-note example and compare which interval is wider.
Find the three notes that change between C major and C natural minor.

A scale places notes in pitch order. Its home note is the tonic. C major is C D E F G A B C, with C as its tonic. The last C is one octave above the first.

In C major, E–F and B–C are half steps; the other gaps are whole steps. Starting on another note preserves the major-scale pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. To keep these gaps, G major uses F♯ and F major uses B♭. Each of the seven notes uses a different letter name.

C natural minor is C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C. Compared with C major, the third, sixth, and seventh notes are each a half step lower. The displayed ♭3, ♭6, and ♭7 show these changes. Natural minor follows whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole steps. Starting on A gives A B C D E F G A.

Below, choose C and major and listen. Keep C selected and switch to natural minor. Find the three changed names and fretboard positions. Then choose G major and F major to locate F♯ and B♭.
Compare C, Cm, and Cmaj7 and find the changed or added chord tones.

A chord combines notes played together. A basic triad consists of a root, third, and fifth. The root is the chord's reference note; it need not be the lowest sounding note. C major is C E G. Count from C: C is 1, E is 3, and G is 5.

Lower E a half step to get C E♭ G, or Cm, a C minor triad. The m means minor. Comparing C and Cm changes only the third. A major triad rooted on D uses D F♯ A to keep the same intervals.

Adding a seventh makes four different chord tones. Cmaj7, a major seventh chord, is C E G B. C7, a dominant seventh chord, is C E G B♭. Cm7, a minor seventh chord, is C E♭ G B♭. First listen to C and Cm, then compare C and Cmaj7 and find the added note.

Explore the other types after these comparisons. Diminished, dim, lowers the third and fifth of a major triad a half step each. Augmented, aug, raises its fifth a half step. Half-diminished seventh, m7♭5, lowers the fifth of a minor seventh chord a half step. Diminished seventh, dim7, lowers the seventh of a half-diminished chord another half step. The displayed ♭♭7 means two half steps below degree 7 of the root's major scale.

Below, choose C as the root and change only the type. Read the note names and degrees. The fretboard locates each chord tone; all its marked positions are not a single fingering to press together.
Connect C, Dm, and G in C major with tonic, predominant, and dominant roles.

C major is a key centered on C that uses the C-major scale. Diatonic chords use only these notes. Take alternate notes from C D E F G A B: C E G makes a C chord. Starting on D gives D F A, a Dm chord.

Building a triad on each note gives C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, Bdim. Their Roman numerals are I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°. The numeral counts from the key's tonic to the chord's root. Capitals mean major, lowercase means minor, and ° means diminished.

A function is a chord's role in a progression. I has tonic function, the home to return to. ii and IV commonly have predominant function, preparing V. V and vii° have dominant function, tending toward home. The display also groups iii and vi as supporting tonic harmony. Their actual roles can change with the surrounding chords and musical context.

Below, choose C major and select C, Dm, and G in turn. Read their Roman numerals and functions and listen. The key's tonic stays C, but the root of Dm is D. With Dm selected, the tone degrees count from D: D is 1, F is ♭3, and A is 5. Distinguish a chord's place in the key from its own tone degrees.
Translate I–IV–V–I into chord names in C major and G major.

A chord progression plays chords in a chosen order. In C major, C, F, G, C is I–IV–V–I. I is the tonic chord, IV prepares the dominant, and V is the dominant tending back to the tonic. Listen for the last C returning to the opening home chord.

Roman numerals show which major-scale note is each chord's root. Moving I–IV–V–I to G major gives G, C, D, G. The chord names change while the numbered relationships stay the same. Both the order and the time spent on each chord affect what you hear.

Another example, I–V–vi–IV, is C, G, Am, F in C major, a common repeating pattern. Lowercase vi means the minor chord Am. ii–V–I is Dm, G, C: predominant, dominant, tonic.

Below, choose C major and I–IV–V–I. Select each chord to inspect its tones. Tap Listen to example to hear the whole progression. Then change the key to G and compare the Roman numerals and chord names. In the Progressions tool, you can choose your own order and chord lengths to practice.
Compare the notes of C, G, and F major and find the relative minor of C major.

The circle of fifths shows relationships between major keys. One clockwise step from C reaches G. The perfect fifth C–G spans seven half steps. The counterclockwise neighbor F is a perfect fourth, five half steps, above C.

C major uses C D E F G A B. G major changes only F to F♯, and F major changes only B to B♭. Each shares six notes with C major. These examples show why neighboring keys are closely related.

The inner labels show relative minor keys. A relative minor's natural minor scale shares its major scale's notes but has a different tonic. C major and A natural minor use the same notes, centered on C and A respectively. The relative minor of G major is E minor.

Select C, G, and F on the circle in turn. Inspect the note names and changed fretboard positions and listen. Find Am inside C as well. One side of the circle uses flat names. When keys such as F♯ major and G♭ major sound alike but use different written names, read the spelling for the displayed key.
Strum Em once per beat for four beats and compare the gaps between sounds.

Strumming plays a chord by sweeping a pick across several strings. In standard tuning, string 6 is low E and string 1 is high E. A downstroke moves from the string-6 side toward string 1; an upstroke moves back.

Hold the pick lightly and relax your wrist. A pick pushed deeply between the strings can catch, so use a small movement with just its tip touching them. Different chords use different strings; the Em below uses all six.

A strum sounds chord tones in a brief sweep. Downstrokes may bring out lower strings, and light upstrokes may bring out upper strings. Compare with picking each string separately and listen to how the tones connect.

Em means E minor. Put your middle finger on string 5, fret 2, and your ring finger on string 4, fret 2. Leave the other strings open. Pick each string separately first to check whether a finger blocks a neighboring string.\n\nSet the metronome to 60 BPM. Count 1, 2, 3, 4 and play one downstroke per beat. D in the TAB means downstroke. Listen for equal gaps between the four strums. Then add one upstroke between each pair of beats and keep your hand moving back and forth evenly.
Alternate downstrokes and upstrokes on one string and compare six notes for timing and volume.

Picking sounds a note by striking a string with a pick. Alternate picking switches between a downstroke and an upstroke for each note. Play only one string; a downstroke moves toward the string-1 side, and an upstroke toward string 6.

Use a small movement so the pick stays close to the string. Prepare the fretting finger before the pick meets the string so the intended note sounds at that moment. Check whether you also hit a neighboring string.

Each picked note has a clear beginning. You do not need to make every downstroke louder. Compare repeated downstrokes with alternating strokes and listen for changes in the gaps or volume.

First alternate downstrokes and upstrokes on the open first string. D in the TAB means downstroke and U means upstroke. When the pick hits just that string, add the sequence open, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1. For the five fretted notes after the open string, use index, middle, ring, middle, index fingers.\n\nAt 60 BPM, play one note per beat with D, U, D, U, D, U. Listen for even gaps and volume across all six notes. If notes cut out or the pick catches, lower the tempo and try a smaller movement.
Sound a second note without picking again and compare how the two notes connect.

Hammer-ons and pull-offs sound a second note on the same string without picking again. For a hammer-on, pick the lower-fret note, then bring another finger onto a higher fret while the string rings. A higher fret has a larger fret number.

For a pull-off, keep the lower-fret finger pressed while removing the higher-fret finger. Give the string a small pluck as that finger leaves so the lower note sounds. Simply lifting it can make the second note too quiet. Do not pull the string far enough to leave the edge of the fretboard.

Compared with picking both notes, the second note has no new pick sound. First check whether it is audible. Adjust finger placement and timing rather than using a lot of force.

Keep your index finger on string 1, fret 5 throughout the exercise. h means hammer-on and p means pull-off. 5h7 means pick fret 5, then bring your ring finger onto fret 7. 7p5 means pick fret 7, then remove your ring finger with a small pluck to return to fret 5.\n\nAt 60 BPM, pick fret 5 on beat 1 and hammer on at beat 2. Pick fret 7 on beat 3 and pull off at beat 4. Listen for the second note staying audible. Then pick all four notes and compare how they connect.
Connect a note from fret 5 to fret 7 with one pick stroke and a slide.

A slide connects two notes by moving the fretting finger to another fret on the same string. Pick the first note, then move without lifting the finger. Press only enough to keep the string ringing. Moving toward larger fret numbers raises the pitch.

Stop just beside the destination metal fret, on the side toward smaller fret numbers. Excess pressure makes movement harder, so use only what you need. Follow the same string without pushing neighboring strings sideways.

Picking both notes gives each a separate beginning. A slide connects them with the sound of the movement between them. Check the arrival pitch first; some fret noise is normal.

First pick C at fret 5 and D at fret 7 on string 3 separately and listen. Put your ring finger at fret 5, pick once, then move the same finger to fret 7. / in the TAB marks a slide to a higher pitch.\n\nAt 60 BPM, pick fret 5 on one beat and arrive at fret 7 on the next. Compare the arriving D with the D you picked separately. Pause, return to fret 5, and repeat.
Compare a bent note at fret 7 with the target pitch at fret 9.

Bending raises a note by pushing or pulling the fretted string across the width of the fretboard. The extra string tension raises its pitch. Unlike a slide, your finger stays at the same fret.

When fretting with your ring finger, support it with your index and middle fingers on lower frets of the same string. Use a small wrist movement instead of pushing hard with one finger. In the string-2 exercise below, push toward string 6 so the string moves away from the fretboard edge.

The arriving pitch matters more than how far you push. Play the target separately first and compare. Begin with a small bend and stop if your hand hurts. Do not force the string to reach the target.

First pick fret 9 on string 2 to hear the target. Put your ring finger at fret 7, middle finger at fret 6, and index finger at fret 5 on that string. Pick fret 7 and make a small bend toward string 6 with all three fingers supporting it.\n\nThe b in 7b9 means bend. Start at fret 7 and aim for the pitch of fret 9, two frets or a whole step higher. It does not tell you to move your finger to fret 9. Compare with the target within a comfortable range, then release gently to the original fret-7 pitch. If the full bend is difficult, practice smaller bends first.
Compare a sustained note without vibrato with the same note using repeated small bends.

Vibrato repeatedly makes small pitch changes to a sustained note. In this exercise, make a small bend to raise the pitch, then return to the original pitch. Repeat while the note rings without picking again each time.

A single bend focuses on reaching a target pitch. Vibrato focuses on the width of the change and the gaps between returns. Start with slow, narrow movements and listen for whether you keep returning to the original note.

Support the fretting finger with nearby fingers and relax your wrist. Return to the original pitch each time instead of raising it further with every movement. If your hand becomes uncomfortable, stop and reduce the force and movement.

Fret string 2 at fret 7 with your ring finger. Support it with your index and middle fingers at lower frets on the same string. First pick once and let the note ring unchanged for four beats at 60 BPM to hear its starting pitch.\n\nPick again. For four beats, gently push the string toward string 6 and return once per beat. ~ in the TAB means vibrato. Listen for a return to the original pitch each time and similar width and spacing across the four movements. Compare with the note without vibrato.
Shorten an open note with palm muting while keeping its pitch audible.

Palm muting uses the picking hand to reduce a string's ringing. The bridge supports the strings on the guitar body. Rest the little-finger edge of your hand lightly on the strings just in front of the bridge, then play with the pick.

Moving the hand slightly away from the bridge toward the fretboard, or pressing more, reduces the ringing. Moving too far or pressing too hard can block the pitch completely. Leave room for the pick to move and use just enough contact to keep the pitch audible.

Compare the long ringing sound with your hand lifted to the shorter, muffled palm-muted sound. Using the same string and tempo first makes the effect of hand placement easier to hear.

First keep the edge of your hand off the strings and play the open low E, string 6. At 60 BPM, use one downstroke per beat for four beats and listen to it ring. Then repeat four strokes with the edge of your hand lightly touching the string near the bridge. PM in the TAB means palm muting.\n\nCompare the beginning and ringing length of the two sounds. Check whether you can still hear the E pitch when muting. If the sound is blocked, reduce the pressure or move the contact point toward the bridge and try again.
